technique: the exit — leaving on an image instead of a statement
lesson:
Today we work on one tool: the exit. The exit means the poem's last picture is a thing you can see, not a statement that tells you what to think.

Look at the end. The poem could have stopped on "a day's not made by what you've stored"—that's a statement, a lesson in words. Instead it keeps going to "pull on your boots" and "go find it fresh." Those are actions and an object. You see boots. You see a man leaving the house.

It works because a picture stays in your head longer than a sentence that explains. When the poem ends on the boots, you watch him move. You feel the day open up, because you're looking at a body about to go outside, not at an idea.

Try this: write your last line as one thing a person does with their hands or feet.

The second time, wait for the boots and notice you can see them.

Here is the poem.
poem:
On the sill a row of jars still waits for lids,
the vinegar in them going sharp and amber,
garlic and the gold root grated raw,
all of it biting the air of the cold kitchen.
You'll want more of the one that burns the throat—
the kind that wakes a man clean through by noon.
There's a farm up the road with ginger put by,
frozen hard as a nail, and a man who'll trade it
for the price of a visit before the light goes.
The hills hold their gray like a thing agreed on.
You pull the one jar close and thumb its rim,
knowing a day's not made by what you've stored—

There's something good to go gather today—
pull on your boots and go find it fresh.
